1.rendering: The pericope opens with the address up front — »Verehrter Theophilus!« — and renders the Greek historian-style preamble in a deliberately elevated, formal register that stands apart from the everyday tone of the rest of the book (»es unternommen, einen zusammenhängenden Bericht über all das niederzuschreiben, was sich unter uns erfüllt und vollendet hat«). The κράτιστε honorific is carried by »hochverehrter Theophilus« in v3, preserving the social transaction of a patron dedication.
1.tradeOff: We deliberately do NOT smooth the prologue into the colloquial register HFA uses; we keep the literary contrast with the rest of Luke so the reader feels a Greek preface, even at the cost of a heavier opening sentence.

3.rendering: »hochverehrter Theophilus« preserves the κράτιστε social marker — Theophilus is being addressed as a person of high standing, the kind of patron a work is dedicated to, not merely a friend.
3.tradeOff: No clean modern German equivalent for κράτιστε exists; »hochverehrter« risks sounding stiff, but a flatter »lieber« would erase the honor-transaction the reviewer asked us to retain.

4.rendering: Rendered »wie verlässlich und fundiert das ist, worin man dich unterwiesen hat« — switching the earlier »fester Grund« metaphor to »fundiert« as the reviewer requested, paired with »verlässlich« for the ἀσφάλεια nuance of secure, examined truth.
4.tradeOff: »fundiert« leans intellectual rather than foundational-architectural; we lose a faint building metaphor but gain modern idiom.

5.rendering: Rather than just naming the Abijah course and Aaronic descent, the body unpacks the social inference: »In dieser Familie kam das Priesteramt von beiden Seiten zusammen, und jeder im Land hätte gesagt: Solche Menschen stehen Gott besonders nahe, auf ihnen muss sein Segen liegen.« This sets up the tension Luke will then break in v7 — the village would have assumed automatic divine favor for a doubly-priestly couple.
5.tradeOff: Longer than a literal rendering, and risks editorializing; but without it the modern reader cannot feel why their childlessness becomes a public scandal in v7. The reviewer specifically flagged that »ansah« did not transport this connection.

6.rendering: Replaced the archaic »rechtschaffen« with »lebten die beiden so, wie es vor Gott recht ist: Sie hielten sich an alles, was der Herr geboten hatte, und niemand konnte ihnen etwas vorwerfen« — keeping the legal-covenantal sense (commandments observed, blameless) while using modern, accessible idiom.
6.tradeOff: Loses the single-word punch of »fromm«/»rechtschaffen«; gains transparency and avoids the archaism the reviewer flagged.

7.rendering: The body keeps the bare fact (»Sie hatten kein Kind«) but then adds the village's voice: »Und mancher fragte sich im Stillen, was sie wohl verschuldet hatten, dass Gott ihnen ein Kind versagte.« This makes the honor/shame stigma — the public suspicion that childlessness was divine punishment — audible to a modern reader who would otherwise miss the social weight of v5–7.
7.tradeOff: We are voicing a community judgment Luke only implies; some readers will hear it as interpretive overlay. But the rationale flags this as a must-land friction, and the alternative is a flat clinical statement of infertility.

9.rendering: Added the explicit gloss »Für die meisten Priester kam dieser Augenblick im ganzen Leben nur ein einziges Mal.« — making the unique social honor of being chosen by lot to burn incense felt by the reader instead of left to a footnote.
9.tradeOff: Adds a sentence Luke himself does not write; but the rationale lists this as a must-land cultural fact, and without it the drama of v11 (an angel meeting Zechariah here, of all moments) collapses.

12.rendering: »erschrak er bis ins Mark; die nackte Angst überfiel ihn« — answering the reviewer's request for a rendering that carries the bodily force of the fear (erzitterte / war erschüttert) rather than a polite »erschrak«.
12.tradeOff: Two clauses where Greek has a compact phrase; risks slight melodrama. Chosen because Luke is reporting a man's whole body reacting, and a single mild verb flattens that.

14.rendering: »Freude und Glück« in place of the older »Jubel«, per the reviewer's note that Jubel sounds dated. The doubling keeps the warmth of both χαρά and ἀγαλλίασις without reaching for archaic vocabulary.
14.tradeOff: Loses the celebratory loudness of »Jubel«; gains a register that an actual modern father would recognize.

15.rendering: »Denn in Gottes Augen wird er ein Großer sein. Wein wird er nicht trinken, auch nichts anderes, was berauscht.« — following the HFA-style dynamic equivalence the reviewer requested, instead of the more literal »weder Wein noch berauschendes Getränk«.
15.tradeOff: Drops the technical pair (oinos / sikera) into a single modern phrasing; loses the Nazirite-vow echo for readers who would catch it, gains immediate comprehensibility.

16.rendering: »zum Herrn, ihrem Gott, zurückbringen« — keeps the prophetic return language plainly, without archaism.
16.tradeOff: none — the verse is straightforward and the rendering does not over-interpret.

17.rendering: »Mit der Kraft und dem Geist des Propheten Elija« — switched »Wucht« to »Kraft« per reviewer, with »des Propheten« added so the name lands for readers without footnote knowledge. The Malachi echo is rendered intersectionally as »Eltern und Kinder wieder zueinander« rather than gendered »Väter und Söhne«, and the rest is loosened into modern syntax: »führt die, die sich Gott verschließen, zurück zu der Einsicht, nach der man recht vor Gott lebt.«
17.tradeOff: »Eltern und Kinder« weakens the direct Malachi 4:5–6 lexical echo (»Väter zu den Söhnen«) for readers tracking the OT allusion; we judged inclusivity and modern accessibility worth that loss, per the reviewer's question about whether the gendered language was warranted.

18.rendering: »Wie kann ich sicher sein, dass das wirklich geschieht?« replaces the wooden »Woran soll ich erkennen, dass es so kommt?« the reviewer flagged. Reads as a normal old man's question, not a liturgical formula.
18.tradeOff: Loses the literal »knowing-by-sign« nuance of κατὰ τί γνώσομαι; gains the natural human voice the moment requires.

20.rendering: Opens with »Aber weil du meinen Worten nicht geglaubt hast« — the English-calque »Doch nun:« the reviewer flagged is gone; the sentence is restructured around the cause (unbelief) and effect (silence) in natural German prose.
20.tradeOff: Loses the abrupt ἰδού (»look!«) shift at the head of the verse; gains a sentence that reads as German rather than translated Greek.

23.rendering: »Als seine Dienstzeit zu Ende war, ging er nach Hause.« — the reviewer flagged »Als die Tage seines Dienstes...« as old-fashioned biblical. The new rendering uses ordinary modern phrasing.
23.tradeOff: Loses the Hebraic »days of his service« cadence; the verse is a transition, not a poetic peak, so we judged accessibility worth more than rhythm here.

25.rendering: Substantially rewritten per the reviewer's strong feedback: »So hat der Herr an mich gedacht und mir geholfen. Jetzt nimmt er mir die Schande, weil ich kein Kind bekommen konnte. Niemand kann mich mehr dafür verachten.« — closer to the HFA dynamic move, naming explicitly what »angesehen« meant (God remembered her, acted, took away the public scorn).
25.tradeOff: More words than the original Greek; loses the slightly cryptic interiority of »ἐπεῖδεν ἀφελεῖν«. Gains the meaning the reviewer said the comparison step should already have caught: this is Elizabeth's public vindication, not a private mystical murmur.

26.rendering: Spelling normalized to »Nazareth« per the reviewer (not »Nasaret«). The body then adds the class/marginality gloss »Ein Ort, von dem kaum jemand je gehört hatte.« — making the reversal-theme starting condition (»the Most High chooses a peasant girl from nowhere«) visible to a modern reader.
26.tradeOff: Adds a sentence the Greek does not have; risks editorializing. But without it, »Nazareth« is just a foreign place-name and the social shock of God choosing this village is lost.

27.rendering: Added »sie wohnte weiter bei ihrer Familie, bis Josef das gemeinsame Zuhause fertig hätte« per the reviewer's suggestion — explaining the betrothal customs so the modern reader understands the social setup that makes vv34–35 so dangerous (Mary still in her father's house, Joseph still preparing theirs).
27.tradeOff: Goes beyond what Luke says; some readers will hear it as historical reconstruction. But the rationale flags purity-boundary friction as must-land, and the household geography is the key to feeling it.

32.rendering: »den Thron seines Vorfahren David« — »Vorfahren« per reviewer, since »Vater« would mislead modern readers into thinking of David as Jesus' literal father rather than his royal ancestor.
32.tradeOff: Loses the Greek/Hebrew idiomatic use of »father« for any forebear; gains genealogical clarity.

33.rendering: »über das Volk Israel herrschen, über alle, die von Jakob abstammen« — the reviewer noted »Haus Jakob« is not immediately clear; the rendering unpacks the metonymy into »the people of Israel, all who descend from Jacob« so the connection lands.
33.tradeOff: Loses the OT idiom »house of Jacob« that connects this prophecy to its Hebrew Bible roots; gains immediate intelligibility.

34.rendering: Significantly amplified: »Wie soll das geschehen? Ich habe doch noch mit keinem Mann geschlafen. Und wenn ich schwanger werde, bevor Josef und ich zusammenleben, wer wird mir dann glauben? Man wird mich für eine Ehebrecherin halten. Josef kann mich verstoßen, und nach dem Gesetz kann man eine wie mich sogar steinigen.« — making the must-land friction (capital-offense-level social danger of pregnancy during betrothal) audible inside the running text rather than relegated to a footnote.
34.tradeOff: We are voicing Mary's interior calculus where Luke only writes »ἐπεὶ ἄνδρα οὐ γινώσκω«. Risks reading as expansion. Justified by the rationale: without the stakes, modern readers hear an angelic visitation as wonderful news rather than as the start of a crisis.

38.rendering: Prefaced with »Maria wusste, was ihr Ja sie kosten konnte: den Verdacht des Dorfes, die Schande ihrer Familie, vielleicht Josefs Bruch mit ihr.« before the canonical line »Ich gehöre Gott und stehe ihm zur Verfügung. Mit mir soll geschehen, was du gesagt hast.« This makes Mary's faith-response visibly costly — the virtue is the courage to say yes against the stakes named in v34, not a vague pious docility.
38.tradeOff: Adds a full sentence of inner monologue Luke does not write. We accept the interpretive risk because the rationale explicitly warns against »virginity ideology« readings that locate Mary's virtue in physical state rather than faith-response.

39.rendering: »Kurz darauf machte sich Maria auf den Weg und eilte in eine Stadt im Bergland von Judäa.« — drops the Lutheran-archaic »in jenen Tagen« per the reviewer; »eilte« carries the σπουδή, »Bergland« stands in for ὀρεινή without the militaristic »Tagesmärsche« the reviewer also flagged.
39.tradeOff: Loses the formal narrative opening of the Greek; gains a clean modern sentence appropriate to the story's emotional momentum.

43.rendering: »Wer bin ich, dass die Mutter meines Herrn zu mir kommt?« replaces the archaic »Wie geschieht mir« the reviewer flagged. Keeps the genuine astonishment and the honor-reversal (the elder priestly wife deferring to the younger peasant girl) in fully modern German.
43.tradeOff: Loses the literal πόθεν (»from where«) idiom; gains a sentence that actually sounds like astonishment to a modern ear.

44.rendering: »Denn kaum hörte ich deine Stimme, da sprang das Kind in mir vor Freude auf.« — »Leib« is dropped per reviewer (»Leib is an outdated term«); the verse follows the HFA-style dynamic move the reviewer pointed to, expressing meaning over literal lexicon.
44.tradeOff: Loses the formal »fruit of your womb« register; gains modern, embodied language that actually reads as a pregnant woman describing her own body.

50.rendering: »zu allen, die ihm mit offenem Herzen begegnen, Generation um Generation.« — replaces the archaic »die ihn fürchten« the reviewer flagged, while finding a modern poetic phrase rather than copying HFA's »in Ehrfurcht vor ihm leben«. The repetition »Generation um Generation« carries εἰς γενεὰς καὶ γενεάς.
50.tradeOff: Loses the lexical link to OT »fear of the LORD« language; some readers will miss the covenantal register. The reviewer judged that loss worth modernizing the line.

51.rendering: »Er hat mit bloßem Arm seine Kraft gezeigt: die Hochmütigen mit all ihren stolzen Plänen hat er in alle Winde zerstreut.« — picks up the HFA pattern the reviewer pointed to (»fegt … hinweg«) while keeping our own poetic register (»mit bloßem Arm«, »in alle Winde zerstreut«). The cosmic-reversal force the rationale calls for is in the verbs.
51.tradeOff: Slightly more concrete (»in alle Winde zerstreut«) than the Greek's »scattered them in the imagination of their hearts« — we abandon the διανοίᾳ καρδίας idiom and instead lift »stolzen Plänen« forward, which is the modern poetic equivalent.

53.rendering: »mit leeren Händen weggeschickt« per the reviewer's preference over a bare »Leer.« — the German idiom »mit leeren Händen« is the natural counterweight to »reich beschenkt« in the previous line, sustaining the economic-reversal pair.
53.tradeOff: none — the idiom is standard German and preserves the chiastic pairing.

54.rendering: »Er hat sich seines Volkes Israel angenommen und sein Erbarmen nicht vergessen« — collapses Israel-as-παῖς into the dynamic »Volk Israel«, since »seines Dieners« sounded archaic to the reviewer and clouded the corporate sense (Israel as servant, not an individual servant Israel).
54.tradeOff: Loses the Isaianic Servant echo (παῖς αὐτοῦ Ἰσραήλ); a Bible-literate reader will miss the Servant Songs allusion. Judged worth it for the modern register.

60.rendering: »Nein. Er soll Johannes heißen.« — the curt »Nein.« as its own sentence carries the social shock the rationale flags: a woman publicly overriding her relatives' naming proposal would have been startling. The body lets that surprise sit before the name is given.
60.tradeOff: Greek has οὐχί but the rendering's punctuated brevity is a deliberate dramatic choice; risks reading as terse, which is exactly the point.

63.rendering: »Sein Name ist Johannes.« — written, not spoken, in the simple indicative the Greek has (ἐστὶν, not future). Zechariah confirms what Elizabeth already said; the community's astonishment that follows is the tension-resolving beat the rationale names.
63.tradeOff: none — the rendering tracks the Greek and preserves the dramatic moment cleanly.

68.rendering: »Er ist zu seinem Volk gekommen und hat den Preis bezahlt, der uns freikauft.« — the technical λύτρωσις is rendered with the concrete ransom-payment image (»den Preis bezahlt, der uns freikauft«) rather than a flat »erlöst«, so a modern reader hears the price-and-release dynamic.
68.tradeOff: Two clauses where Greek has the noun ἐποίησεν λύτρωσιν; gains concreteness, loses the noun-phrase compactness. The image carries the OT redemption theology better than an abstract »Erlösung«.

70.rendering: »genau wie er es vor langer Zeit durch den Mund seiner heiligen Propheten zugesagt hat« — »vor langer Zeit« replaces the archaic »von alters her« the reviewer flagged, while keeping the prophets-of-old register.
70.tradeOff: Loses the timeless, hieratic feel of »von alters her«; gains a phrase a modern reader actually parses.

78.rendering: »So tief geht das Erbarmen unseres Gottes, dass es ihn im Innersten ergreift.« — the visceral σπλάγχνα ἐλέους (»bowels of mercy«) is rendered as »im Innersten ergreift«, holding the gut-level depth without using the anatomical Greek metaphor literally.
78.tradeOff: Loses the body-organ vividness of σπλάγχνα; gains a phrase that lands in modern German without sounding either clinical or pious-archaic.

78.rendering: »Darum kommt er zu uns, der aus der Höhe aufgeht, einer, der über uns hereinbricht wie ein neuer Morgen« — the ambiguous ἀνατολή (rising star / branch / dawn) is rendered with the dawn image, doubled (»aufgeht«, »wie ein neuer Morgen«) so the poetry breaks open rather than reading as a flat metaphor.
78.tradeOff: Closes off the »branch« reading (Jer 23:5 / Zech 3:8) in favor of the dawn reading that flows naturally into v79's »leuchtet … im Dunkeln«. A Bible-literate reader loses the Davidic-branch echo.

80.rendering: »Das Kind wuchs heran, und Gottes Geist machte es stark. Johannes lebte fern von allem, draußen in der Einöde, bis zu dem Tag, an dem er offen vor Israel hervortrat.« — a single-sentence summary that leaves the rationale's »What will this child become?« open into chapter 3, with plain modern vocabulary throughout.
80.tradeOff: none — the verse is a transition and does not need amplification.
